name: PF-08653945

lead: PF-08653945 (also MET-233i) is an investigational amylin analogue for weight management, listed as being developed by Pfizer. People follow it for fullness-driven fat loss.

Amylin analogues mimic a pancreatic hormone involved in satiety and slower digestion, so the chain is greater fullness, lower intake, then weight loss and a leaner body. A 2026 narrative review describes the class as an emerging approach that complements incretin-based drugs; no human trial results for this compound are published.

paras: It is available only in clinical research settings.
Human safety data are not public. It is not approved.

angle.text: PF-08653945 is Pfizer's early-stage amylin analogue, followed by fat-loss readers as a fullness-based route to a leaner body. It mimics a satiety hormone to cut intake. No effects have been published yet.

lead: PF-08653945, formerly MET-233i, is an investigational amylin analogue for weight management, now developed by Pfizer after its acquisition of Metsera. It is not approved.[1] Its appearance relevance is through fat loss: amylin analogues aim to reduce appetite and body weight, which people pursue for a leaner body and face.

Pfizer describes MET-233i as a monthly amylin analogue candidate in Phase 1 development, being evaluated alone and in combination with the incretin candidate MET-097i; initial Phase 1 results were presented at the 61st EASD Annual Meeting on 17 September 2025, and the acquisition was announced on 22 September 2025.[1]
It belongs to the amylin analogue class, which a 2026 narrative review describes as an emerging therapeutic approach to obesity complementing incretin-based drugs.[2]

paras: Metsera developed MET-233i; Pfizer announced in September 2025 that it would acquire the company. Pfizer's release lists MET-233i as a monthly amylin analogue in Phase 1, studied as monotherapy and combined with MET-097i.[1]

No peer-reviewed results for PF-08653945 have been located. Initial Phase 1 results of MET-233i were presented at the EASD meeting in September 2025.[1] A 2026 review covers amylin-based therapies in obesity more broadly, including early-phase trials of the class.[2]

timeline.event: Initial Phase 1 results for MET-233i presented at EASD (17 September); Pfizer announces Metsera acquisition (22 September).[1]
